summary: Describes STUN, a lightweight protocol that lets applications discover NATs and firewalls between them and the public Internet, and learn the public IP addresses allocated to them. It was replaced by RFC 5389.

eli5.summary: Behind a home router, a program does not know what address the world sees. STUN asks a helper server to tell it. It was later replaced by RFC 5389.

questions: how to discover public ip behind nat
how do i find my public ip behind nat
can stun work through symmetric nat
subtitle: Learn your public IP address behind a NAT using a helper server.

tldr.problem: A computer behind a home router or corporate firewall cannot directly see what public IP address the outside world uses to reach it. Without knowing this address, peer-to-peer applications cannot receive incoming connections from the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: STUN provides a lightweight protocol where a client sends a request to a public STUN server, and the server echoes back the client's public IP address and port as seen from the server's perspective. By sending multiple probe requests with different parameters, the client can also determine what type of NAT it is behind.
tldr.outcome: Applications can discover their public Internet address and learn whether they can accept incoming peer-to-peer connections. STUN was later superseded by RFC 5389, which is a more refined specification of the same concept.

today: RFC 3489 was superseded by RFC 5389, which provides a more refined definition of the STUN protocol and is the current standard for discovering addresses behind NATs. The basic concepts remain the same, but RFC 5389 clarifies the protocol and adds improvements.

sections.title: The NAT Problem
sections.content: Network Address Translators (NATs) are essential devices in home and corporate networks. They translate private, non-routable IP addresses used inside a network into public addresses on the Internet, allowing many internal computers to share a single public IP. However, NATs create a challenge for peer-to-peer applications. When a peer-to-peer application behind a NAT wants to receive incoming data from the Internet, it has no way to know what public address and port the NAT has allocated for it. Without this information, the application cannot advertise a working address to its peers. Traditional solutions like Application Layer Gateways (ALGs) embedded in NATs have significant limitations, and waiting for NAT upgrades is impractical. STUN solves this by allowing applications to discover the NAT's address binding directly.
sections.eli5: A home router hides your computer's real address and uses its own address instead. Your program does not know what address the router shows to the Internet, so it cannot tell friends how to reach it. STUN fixes this by asking a server on the Internet to send back what it sees.

sections.title: NAT Types and Behavior
sections.content: STUN defines four categories of NAT behavior that affect whether peer-to-peer communication is possible. A full-cone NAT maps all outgoing packets from an internal address and port to a single public address and port, and allows any external host to send packets to that public address. A restricted-cone NAT is similar but only allows external packets from hosts to which the internal computer has previously sent packets. A port-restricted-cone NAT is even more restrictive, requiring the external sender to match both the IP address and port of a previous outgoing packet. Finally, a symmetric NAT creates different external mappings for each combination of internal address, internal port, and external destination. Symmetric NATs are the most restrictive because only the specific external host that received a packet can send a response back. Understanding which type of NAT is present is crucial because it determines what kinds of peer-to-peer connections are possible.
sections.eli5: Not all routers work the same way when hiding your address. Some let anyone reach you if you sent them a message first. Others only let specific people reach you. And some create completely different addresses for different destinations. STUN helps you figure out which type you have.

sections.title: The Discovery Process
sections.content: STUN discovery uses a simple but elegant flow of three test requests to determine both the presence of a NAT and its type. Test I sends a Binding Request to the server without any special flags. If the MAPPED-ADDRESS attribute in the response matches the client's local socket address and port, there is no NAT. If it does not match, a NAT is present. Test II sends a request with flags asking the server to send the response from a different address and port. If the client receives the response, it knows it is behind a full-cone NAT or an open firewall. If no response arrives, Test III uses the CHANGED-ADDRESS from Test I to determine whether the client is behind a symmetric NAT or a restricted cone NAT. This clever three-test sequence provides complete classification in most cases.
sections.eli5: STUN sends three test messages to figure out the type of router. The first test shows your address. The second test checks if anyone can reach you. The third test (only if needed) checks if you only accept packets from familiar places.

sections.title: Messages and Attributes
sections.content: STUN messages use a simple TLV (Type-Length-Value) format. Every message starts with a 20-byte header containing the message type, message length, and a 128-bit transaction ID used to match requests and responses. The message type can be a Binding Request, Binding Response, Binding Error Response, Shared Secret Request, Shared Secret Response, or Shared Secret Error Response. Following the header are attributes that describe the payload. The MAPPED-ADDRESS attribute, present in Binding Responses, contains the client's public IP address and port as seen by the server. The CHANGED-ADDRESS attribute tells the client which address the server would use if the response were sent from a different location, supporting the NAT type discovery tests. The CHANGE-REQUEST attribute in requests allows clients to ask the server to use different addresses or ports. The MESSAGE-INTEGRITY attribute provides HMAC-based authentication for requests and responses, protecting against spoofing attacks.
sections.eli5: STUN messages are short and simple. Each one says what it is and includes a unique ID so replies match questions. The server's reply includes your public address and tells you if it could send messages from a different place.

sections.title: Security and Threats
sections.content: STUN servers can be targets for attacks where an attacker intercepts a client's Binding Request and injects a forged response with a false MAPPED-ADDRESS, tricking the client into publishing the attacker's address to its peers. This could enable denial-of-service attacks against a target by making many clients send traffic there. However, the 128-bit random transaction ID in each STUN request makes this difficult; an attacker must observe the request to know the transaction ID and create a matching response. STUN protects against some attacks through use of the MESSAGE-INTEGRITY attribute, which requires a shared secret between client and server. Clients can obtain a temporary shared secret from the STUN server using a TLS-protected Shared Secret Request. Additionally, STUN includes the REFLECTED-FROM attribute, which helps servers prevent being used as reflectors in denial-of-service attacks. The specification acknowledges that STUN has limitations and works best in open networks; it cannot enable incoming TCP connections through NAT and does not work behind symmetric NATs or when client and peer are behind the same NAT.
sections.eli5: Bad actors might try to trick a STUN client by sending fake messages. STUN protects against this using random codes that are hard to guess and by having the server sign its replies. However, STUN is not perfect; it does not work in all situations, especially with very restrictive network setups.

fields.name: Message Type
fields.desc: Message type: Binding Request (0x0001), Binding Response (0x0101), etc.

fields.name: Message Length
fields.desc: Total length of attributes (payload), not including the 20-byte header.

fields.name: Transaction ID (part 1)
fields.desc: First 32 bits of the 128-bit random transaction identifier.

fields.name: Transaction ID (part 2)
fields.desc: Second 32 bits of the transaction identifier.

fields.name: Transaction ID (part 3)
fields.desc: Third 32 bits of the transaction identifier.

fields.desc: Fourth 32 bits of the transaction identifier.
